Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the present limit can be set at $2\times 10^{-6}$ for a particular lepton interaction with masses ranging from 125 to 144 MeV, a region that current production searches lack in depth. Combining existing data with optimized detection tools or improved photon rejection techniques can significantly narrow this limit.

In a gyroscopic Sagnac interferometer, typically used for calibrating a gyroscope's angular momentum, a notable spectral shift around anomalies occurs. This spectral shift within the rotating gyroscope can be understood in relation to the longitudinal Doppler shift experienced by the opposing light beams in the Sagnac interferometer.

This work extends the research of Fittouhi and Joseph on the unipotent orbit decomposition of Weierstrass sections $\Delta_\bullet$ within the general linear group $\mathrm{GL}(n)$, specifically focusing on the special linear group $\mathrm{SL}(n)$. Building upon the results of J. Arato, D. Kolinsky, and D. Kolitsch, who investigated the ideal structure of invariants $\mathbb{C}[\Delta_\bullet]^{\mathrm{GL}(n)}$, this study examines how these ideals behave when restricted to $\mathrm{SL}(n)$, a process that involves analyzing Weierstrass sections as algebraic groups acting in a specific way and decomposing orbits under such an action. Moreover, this research further develops results from B. Roberts and $\gamma$-filtrations associated with Orlik-Harris arrangements, as well as root systems of type $B/C$.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

We've developed families of three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial, non-toric terminal Fano varieties of considerable depth, corresponding to 54 distinct mutation classes in the realm of Laurent polynomials. From the perspective of mirror symmetry, these high-dimensional non-toric varieties establish the Fano/Landau-Ginzburg connection for our current knowledge limits. Building upon this foundation, 46 more $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds have been constructed, with their depth spanning between 10 and 19. Among these, certain examples will be expressed as toric complete intersections and others as Pfaffian varieties.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods.

We investigate the concurrent loss of spatial translation and dilation symmetries in a class of models inspired by the Ginzburg-Landau theory, in which the breaking of these symmetries results in the emergence of fractonic modes. The fractrones in this general framework are divided into two categories: self-locked and stationary. The paper describes a lattice model that incorporates both types of modes, where the continuum limit of this model is analyzed using Ginzburg-Landau theory. The mechanism for realizing both self-locked and stationary modes is discussed, and the conditions under which spatial translation and dilation symmetries are identified. The Ginzburg-Landau theory is employed to discuss the phase diagram of this lattice model.

In an inflationary model, with a specific type of $\alpha$-attractor potential, we examine the behavior in the high-$k$ regime, where cosmological perturbations exhibit excessive growth and negative values of the Bardeen potential. This regime facilitates the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs). Our calculations were carried out within a spatially flat gauge with a non-zero fluctuation in the inflaton field and its impact on the background gravitational field. We determined the scalar density fluctuations ($\sigma$), asymmetry ($\beta$), and PBH mass fraction ($f_\mathrm{PBH}$) in relation to specific mass scales. The results indicate that, under certain conditions, there is sufficient PBH mass formation in a particular mass range. If there is sufficient massive PBH formation in $log_{10}(M_/M_{\odot})=3.66-3.74$, then we observe a sufficient contribution to dark matter and a sufficient enhancement in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) power spectrum in a specific $l$ range. The relationship between ascribed parameters and computational values of $\sigma$, $\beta$, and $f_\mathrm{PBH}$ reveals their distinct peaks at different $log_{10}(k/0.0001\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1})$ values. The results indicate that 2-body annihilation of PBHs contributes to the observed microwave background (MB)

Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some right edges as "optional", given they don't lead to leaf nodes. They employed this model to analyze skew Dyck paths. A key aspect studied was the number of deepest nodes in these marked trees. Through explicit generating functions, they obtained insights, revealing the average number of deepest nodes converges to $\frac53$ as the number of nodes increases, which can be contrasted to standard ordered trees with a convergent average of $2$ deepest nodes.

This investigation seeks to examine the capabilities of Informed OCR (iOCR) in accurately capturing vote tabulation data, as the system is designed with an advanced spell-checking feature to correct common errors associated with traditional OCR technology, which the research reveals results in iOCR outperforming traditional OCR methods.

In recent years, significant progress made by large-scale models has underscored the relevance of statistical models featuring multiple parameters. Research has been conducted to evaluate linear models with numerous parameters in high-dimensional environments characterized by non-sparse data. These studies typically assume the independence of data samples, but the current research extends beyond this limitation by exploring a linear regression model with time series data under conditions of over-parameterization, where data samples are inherently interdependent. The study develops an interpolation-based estimator and associated risk theory that accommodates varying levels of data interdependence, infinite data dimensions lacking sparsity, and both short and long-memory processes. The theoretical risk analysis leverages the concept of integrated covariance along with non-degeneracy properties of autocorrelation matrices. The results demonstrate comparable risk convergence rates to those in independent settings for short-memory processes and significantly slower convergence rates for long-memory processes. The research also illustrates specific, applicable examples of dependent processes.

Speech enhancement, a vital component in audio signal processing and the foundation for other advanced technologies like speech recognition and synthesis, is extensively researched. This paper showcases a novel deep learning architecture for speech enhancement. The proposed model innovatively incorporates a comprehensive attention mechanism within a bidirectional sequence-to-sequence framework, leveraging previously unexplored information within each individual frame. This innovative approach is an evolution of previous attention-based RNN methods. The newly designed bidirectional attention-based architecture surpasses its predecessors in terms of speech quality, outperforming OM-LSA, CNN-LSTM, T-GSA and the unidirectional attention-based LSTM baseline in terms of PESQ.

A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. Our research reveals a non-intrusive vulnerability in these systems, where ultrasonic signals can be used to bypass the DPSs, revealing room secrets to anyone nearby. Our findings highlight three key factors influencing successful attacks: differences in air pressure, system differential control, and room differential control. Our experimental results demonstrate successful breaches of two different NPRs with varying differential control systems, and we believe this vulnerability could pose a greater risk as higher bio-safety levels correspond to more virulent pathogens. Our research recommends deploying additional safety measures to prevent such attacks, potentially reducing the need to redesign existing NPRs, which can be expensive and labor-intensive to modify.

A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is risk aversion. To investigate this hypothesis, we conducted experiments using a theoretically sound model of price-resistant storage behavior and further validated it through simulations using real data. Our findings from both models and real-world examples demonstrate a clear link between storage units avoiding risk and price-resistant behavior. According to our results, these units consistently forgo potential profits in periods of low supply but excessively respond to supply spikes, effectively compensating for periods of price-resistant behavior. This research highlights the significance of considering storage units' psychological factors and offers valuable insights for developing more effective market mechanisms.

In quantum systems, superpositions of electronic states rapidly evolve, 
within the timeframe of few femtoseconds to attoseconds, leading to a charge 
density that varies over time. This work takes advantage of newly produced, 
ultrafast soft x-ray pulses generated by an x-ray free-electron laser to create 
an excitation of core electrons in nitric oxide molecules. Additionally, 
application of an infrared laser pulse in a circular polarization enables the 
creation of a reference point, thus enabling us to study the motion of electrons 
over time and, ultimately, modify this motion by adjusting the photon energy of 
the x-ray pulse. Systems in a state of core excitation provide a crucial framework 
for exploring the coherent electron motion in matter with a high degree of 
precision and an enhanced interaction with light.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, when the curvature of the planet is considered. Baroclinic waves that behave similarly to those observed on Mars appear under specific conditions of temperature differences and atmospheric stability. Extremely fast planetary rotation leads to the formation of multiple jet streams on the poles, similar to the multiple jet patterns observed in gas giant atmospheres, and results in varying distributions of heat in the atmosphere with different rotation speeds.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) benefit from being trained on optimal subsets of annotated data. Active learning algorithms effectively achieve this by pinpointing data samples that are essential for improving DNN performance. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings, where labeling costs can be exorbitant. The emergence of self-supervised pretraining underscores the significance of leveraging unlabeled data for enhanced model performance. Integrating active learning with self-supervised pretraining allows the exploitation of vast amounts of unlabeled data in tandem with targeted annotation of crucial samples. 

In this research, we introduce a novel co-adaptation framework, consisting of a multi-stage process: an initial unsupervised filtering phase, a multi-stage classification training process, and a final fine-tuning step using a smaller dataset of labeled data. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, where minimal annotation efforts yield substantial performance improvements. Specifically, our framework outperformed traditional active learning and self-supervised pretraining approaches. Notably, by annotating just 500 samples, our method outpermed baseline active learning by nearly 10% on the Food10-0 dataset.

This study discloses novel analytical and geometrical aspects of the generalized algebraic multiplicity $\chi$ previously developed in cited works. Notably, it identifies a novel correlation between $\chi$ and local intersection points in algebraic varieties, a pivotal concept in Algebraic Geometry. The relationship between Nonlinear Spectral Theory and Algebraic Geometry gives $\chi$ profound geometric significance. Additionally, $\chi$ is now defined through a local determinant of the Schur operator associated with a linear path $\mathfrak{L}(\lambda)$.

We suggest creating bosonic pairs using large numbers of dipoles with complex internal structures, which interact with an isolated optical cavity. A rapid growth of entanglement between these dipoles arises due to the virtual exchange of photons, resulting in two-mode squeezing. We can relate this phenomenon to optical homodyne measurements by applying transformations and observing changes in the electronic states. We propose using this connection to improve the detection of phase shifts between light signals. We present an example based on strontium atoms and show that our approach remains resilient to errors commonly found in this type of system. Our plan offers potential breakthroughs in entanglement research with atoms and could contribute to the development of more precise optical clocks.

Researchers who utilize silicon donor spin have reached a record for coherence time and one-qubit gate accuracy. To advance further, demonstrating the ability to execute reliable two-qubit logic operations with a strong coupling between qubits, specifically through exchange interaction, is crucial. To facilitate efficient development of large-scale quantum processors, a computational model of two-electron behavior has been created by applying a configuration interaction approach based on a multi-valley effective mass theory. By utilizing the code's efficiency to handle computational demands, exchange interaction effects, valley distribution, and electron distribution were examined in a range of positions, orientations, and under applied electric fields. The findings are displayed in an interactive format that shows donor placement's impact on the behavior of valley and orbital components. The research yields a practical understanding and accurate prediction of necessary conditions to execute reliable two-qubit operations with silicon-based quantum processors.

Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework.

Wireless communication systems can make significant contributions to preventing road accidents through alert message transmission, particularly in high-risk areas like road intersections. Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) has shown promise for 5G systems, and our proposed adaptive cooperative NOMA (ACN) protocol enhances VC's performance in this area. In a scenario where vehicles on intersecting roads generate interfering signals, we develop a mathematical model for calculating the outage probability of the ACN protocol and provide analytical expressions for the results. By comparing the ACN protocol to existing alternatives, we demonstrate that ACN yields a substantial improvement in outage probability at road intersections, particularly for higher data transfer rates. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations verify our theoretical findings.

In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference.

Despite numerous theories, there has not been a clear understanding of the high-temperature tail observed in the specific heat of type-II superconductors within their transition region. This study presents an unprecedented finding in He II vanadium dioxide, a type-II superconductor, where the high-temperature tail of the specific heat matches exactly the lower-temperature data. We propose that this entire data set can be explained by a vortex lattice containing mobile defect formations. These defects, present in both the superconducting and normal phases of VDO, contribute to a specific heat related to their chemical potential. By applying a simple statistical mechanics approach to this defect formation contribution, we are able to match the observed data.

Researchers suggest employing high-order cumulants and factorial cumulants of conserved charges to investigate critical dynamics in heavy-ion collision experiments. A parametric representation of the 3D Ising model, which shares a universality class with Quantum Chromo-Dynamics, is used in this study to examine how the second to fourth-order cumulant values of the order parameter change with temperature, and regardless of an external magnetic field at the critical temperature, these normalized cumulant values are independent, resulting in a temperature fixed point. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations in finite systems confirm the existence of this fixed point at temperatures near the critical point. The fixed point is also found in normalized factorial cumulant behavior for at least fourth-order cumulants and is mapped into the QCD, resulting in a similar fixed point in energy dependence along different freeze-out curves in QCD.

A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares of C*-algebras, resulting in hyperfinite type II_1 subfactors of finite index and depth, is provided, utilizing Morita equivalent unitary fusion categories. We extend a prior investigation by N. Sato, generalizing his findings to encompass the broader context of such squares. Additionally, we establish a characterization for such squares yielding a given type II_1 subfactor, and this analysis contributes to a broader understanding of 4-tensors related to matrix product operators in 2-dimensional topological systems.

In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility, as we demonstrate. Specifically, we show that the proposed method enables successful learning even when provided with limited or incorrect gradient data. Furthermore, the framework grants us the ability to recover from such scenarios, even when employing an outdated gradient. We have evaluated our method on two widely used benchmark datasets for optimization and hyperparameter learning, and confirmed its superiority to traditional optimization approaches and existing MAML-based methods.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the classifier. We believe this proposed system could serve as a starting point for further exploration into the use of collaborative multi-agent systems in creating more robust and reliable AI applications.

In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of high-quality specialized datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset named AirPort, which contains over 10,000 images and annotates prohibited items along with their bounding boxes. This dataset serves as a crucial benchmark for prohibited item detection in x-ray images. Moreover, we discover an interesting phenomenon in this dataset - the presence of prohibited items can sometimes go undetected due to their low visibility, even when they are located within the same image. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel component called the Lateral Inhibition Module, which incorporates external information into its decision-making process for detecting objects within its own Bounding Box Proposal Module. Furthermore, we observe that traditional prohibited item detection models are susceptible to being influenced by diverse and often irrelevant objects in x-ray images. To mitigate this, we propose an All-in-one Decision Module capable of distinguishing between target and background objects by learning their mutual exclusion relationships. This module significantly enhances object discrimination and contributes to improved detection performance. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving a substantial 8.4% improvement in detection performance compared to existing methods.

A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture for a broad category of pseudo-Anosov links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be expressed as a function, featuring specific properties, which is derived from an action on a modular representation of the fundamental group of the torus minus the link, yielding $D_n$.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.

This study formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a modified hypersingular integral. It also proves the connection to the traditional complex representation, in addition to obtaining a modified complex representation following the standard Hankel path.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold, confirming the observation. Two methods were employed to derive measurement results, with both approaches yielding consistent outcomes. The cross section for top quark pair production was determined to be 10.9 ± 2.8 (statistical) ± 1.6 (systematic) ± 1.6 (luminosity) nanobarns, in line with the predicted value of quantum chromodynamics calculations.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. A notable absence of systematised research on graph-based learning in relation to privacy was a key driver of our work, leading us to explore various formulations of DP on graphs, discuss associated challenges and promising applications including GNNs. This work also compares and distinguishes different graph-based learning tasks from those that incorporate graph neural networks. Ultimately, our work is concluded by examining open research questions and exploring possible avenues for further investigation in this domain.

The vast amount of images, data, and resources that Euclid will generate positions the consortium to create comprehensive legacy databases of outstanding quality, encompassing high-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy with significant implications for the study of galaxies. These proceedings outline the promising opportunities and scientific breakthroughs Euclid will achieve in the areas of galaxy and AGN development, the evolution of the cosmos, investigations of the Milky Way, and various other celestial bodies and phenomena.

In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to veer off its intended path. We validated our method with three distinct search configurations, focusing on balancing testing speed and practicality for simulated evaluations of autonomous lane-keeping systems.

To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist.

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Furthermore, we applied and validated our method by investigating a quantum shock wave scenario using both Monte Carlo simulations and the associated classical stochastic equation.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through an iterative process, refining the proposal by aggregating both short and long-term contextual information. Notably, DCAN achieves this without the need for external motion modules, as it leverages motion context internally to enhance long-term dependency aggregation. Our proposed DCAN has been shown to outperform current state-of-the-art methods on the ActivityNet, THUMOS-14, and DVS datasets. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zw208/DCAN.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. Measuring the currents within these coherent regions has not been feasible until now, but new diagnostic data from the JET OHCRF system during specific discharges allowed for the calculation of the electric field inside magnetic flux tubes. By correlating this data with solitary waves detected using voltmeters, researchers discovered that the current within these flux tubes aligns with the central parallel current of the solitary wave. Surprisingly, the calculation reveals the presence of a concentrated bundle of parallel currents within the plasma turbulence itself, similar to those found in PTM. As a result, this study proposes that the calculation of edge plasma turbulence flows supports the theory that PTM and blob/hole structures are both manifestations of localized bundles of parallel currents embedded within turbulent plasma. Consequently, magnetic field perturbations measured by antenna rows should be interpreted in light of this new understanding, as doing so will provide a clearer picture of the relationship between blob/hole behavior and PTM.

This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds in a two-dimensional space, leveraging dynamic vortex potential fields and their gradients to create cooperative behavior between the robots. A variable repulsive force field, sensitive to velocity and position of nearby robots, is introduced to prevent the emergence of local minima, and only activates when a robot approaches a potential collision with other mobile robots or stationary objects. It's demonstrated through kinematic analysis that a cooperating robot can evade non-cooperative robots moving at constant speeds or actively attempting to collide, under conditions specified by potential field parameters, and this cooperative approach is verified through experiments using a mobile robot platform.

Given an independent and identically distributed sequence of letters broken down into words based on independent and identically distributed renewal times, an independent and identically distributed sequence of words is formed.  The annealed large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical process of words is characterized by a rate function that equals the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of words with respect to the reference distribution of words.  For renewal times with an algebraic tail, a quenched LDP (conditioned on a typical sequence of letters) was established by Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander, which resulted in a rate function consisting of two components, including the annealed rate function and another component proportional to the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of letters relative to the reference distribution of letters, obtained by combining the words and randomizing the starting point.  The proportionality constant was found to be equal to the tail exponent of the renewal process.  The purpose of this study is to extend both LDPs to sequences of letters that are not independent and identically distributed by demonstrating that both principles can be applied to sequences of letters satisfying a condition known as summable variation, which provides the necessary condition for both principles to be applicable, while neither of the reference laws involved in the rate functions is independent and identically distributed.

Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link.

Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. This paper presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods, combining multiple mutations to assess the effectiveness of fuzzers for the first time. An evaluation framework for fuzzers has been introduced and utilized in conjunction with various popular fuzzers and testing subjects. The evaluation results indicate that contemporary fuzzers can detect mutations in only a small percentage, but this outcome serves as a motivation for future research to address (1) the enhancement of fuzzer performance in detecting sophisticated failures and (2) the development of more effective techniques for triggering mutations and faults.

Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a single, unchanged pretrained model can efficiently handle multiple rounds of continual learning. To demonstrate this, we conduct experiments on standard benchmark datasets, comparing our method to state-of-the-art prevention and reversal models. The results indicate that a static pretrained model outperforms both types of dynamic models. To further validate the efficacy of freezing the pretrained model, we examine models with varying degrees of preprocessing and apply them to various deep learning tasks, including zero-shot and few-shot learning.

We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of Jordan curves, and investigate its properties. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space has a certain topological characteristic, maps that are relatively 1-homotopic are also relatively homotopic.

This final installment concludes our comprehensive study of the solutions $u$ to the given semilinear parabolic equation on the real line. These bounded solutions $u$ of the equation $u_t = u_{xx} + f(u)$, where the initial data have distinct finite limits, were examined earlier with specific conditions on the function $f$ being locally Lipschitz on the real line. This time we explore a scenario in which the function $f$ satisfies particular equilibrium conditions, specifically where $\theta^\pm = \theta_0$ and $f(\theta_0) = 0$. However, the condition is that $\theta_0$ should be an unstable equilibrium of the differential equation. This analysis extends our existing theorem for quasiconvergence by removing certain technical conditions, thus making it more flexible in terms of the requirements for solutions $u$. It should be noted that the new condition is that the solution is nonoscillatory at a certain time. This result holds the potential to be optimal as oscillatory solutions may not be quasiconvergent.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked the boundary of this structure.

Approximately nine years ago, Azrieli and Shmaya introduced a category of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games where each player's payoff function is influenced by a $\lambda$-Lipschitz rate in response to other players' actions. Their work demonstrated that these types of games have the capacity for achieving $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$ settings. Despite their findings, they left unanswered the question regarding the complexity of obtaining such equilibrium points. Our work contributes a query-efficient conversion from broader classes of games to those defined as Lipschitz games, thereby allowing us to derive a lower-bound restriction for the efficiency of randomized algorithms in finding $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in $n$-player games with binary actions and specific $\lambda$-Lipschitz properties, with an exponential relationship between the complexity and the ratio of $\frac{n\lambda}{\epsilon}$. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of 'Multi-Lipschitz games' that incorporate distinct Lipschitz rates for each player, followed by a transformation from equilibrium-finding tasks within this broader class to similar tasks within the domain of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, with implications on the sum of individual $\lambda$-Lipschitz parameters. Finally, we establish a lower-bound restriction indicating that deterministic algorithms experience an exponential increase in complexity in finding $\epsilon$-approximate correlated equilibria in $n

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over maximizing assessed performance. In line with this principle, our study advocates for the adoption of reduced variance j-k fold CV, as demonstrated by the findings that the model yielding the lowest standard deviation over 500 independent assessments emerged as the best model, and the associated standard deviations of validation scores for these models were notably lower than those achieved with traditional k-fold CV. Similarly, the standard deviations of KAGGLE house prices prices were reduced when employing reduced variance 10-k fold CV, further underscoring the efficacy of this method.

Deep Neural Networks with vast parameters have faced challenges in real-time deployment, prompting the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in knowledge distillation. Initially used to achieve comparable performance with smaller student networks, these architectures have now been applied across various knowledge learning objectives such as knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Current research leveraging Teacher-Student architectures has successfully combined multiple knowledge-learning objectives with efficient, lightweight student networks. This distinct survey delves into the specifics of Teacher-Student architectures with multiple knowledge learning objectives and systematically explores knowledge construction and optimization processes, as well as analyzing various Teacher-Student architectures and learning schemes that produce robust and representative knowledge. Moreover, the paper summarizes and highlights the practical applications of Teacher-Student architectures across various purposes, such as classification, recognition, and generation, before exploring promising research directions, particularly on the design of Teacher-Student architectures, the quality of knowledge, and the theoretical studies of regression-based learning. With its in-depth analysis, this survey is poised to provide invaluable insights for industry practitioners and the academic community on the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in multiple knowledge learning objectives.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure.

We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam as it passes through a cloud of critically cold atoms. The absorption characteristics are significantly influenced by the interactive cycle of a photon being absorbed, emitting, and potentially absorbing again, which modifies the absorption profile. The effects of this cycle, where a photon affects its own absorption, are taken into account, alongside the effects of Doppler shifts and spontaneous emission, in a study conducted with sodium D2 line atoms. The results of this study are applicable to a range of phenomena, including saturated absorption spectroscopy, Beal's experiment, and the development of low-loss optical devices, such as isolators and diodes. Notably, our model is based on fundamental physics and does not rely on any unproven assumptions.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the ratios of attractive to repulsive forces, the models can be expanded to encompass state-dependent thickening observed in particle mixes with pull-together forces.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. As a result, the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be presented through generators and defining relations, offering an innovative perspective on its structure. Additionally, the series known as the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be computed explicitly. The research discussed also extends towards the special Askey-Wilson algebra as well as more complex, higher rank variants of the same, allowing further exploration of its properties through tensor products.

Our study shows that in a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet, low-lying triplon
excitations may be responsible for observing magnetic analogs of twisted superfluid and
supersolid phases, particularly when Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions are strong, as
seen in TlCuCl3 and similar materials. Using the supersymmetric Su-Schrieffer-Heferberg
model, we find the required DM interactions vary based on the ratio of weak and strong
couplings, an anisotropy factor, and a chemical potential for energy, with specific
thresholds necessary for twisted phase stability. Our path integral Monte Carlo
simulations support this view, demonstrating that magnetic twisted phases are more
feasible than their nonmagnetic counterparts.

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-scattered nuclei, specifically examining how the incident velocity of these particles influences the scattering probability as they interact with target nuclei across various recoil angles and narrow energy ranges. Our simulation reveals that not only do the incident velocity characteristics of halo WIMPs play a crucial role, but so does the angle of the recoil itself, resulting in an irregular correlation of the two in specific energy ranges. Consequently, attempting to infer the 1-dimensional velocity distribution within these ranges directly from the overall WIMP halo velocities may not provide a complete or accurate understanding, which would ultimately distort our calculations of the associated scattering event rates in those particular ranges.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search to perform their knowledge work and expository writing tasks. According to the study, which involved observing and interviewing 10 participants, Google's Web search algorithm created filter bubbles that limited the information these officials encountered on the Web. This study contributes to the broader understanding of how search engines influence our lives and poses potential risks, with as much as 40% of relevant information that could have been found online going unnoticed. Additionally, the study offers new evidence for real-world applications of Google's Web search algorithm and highlights the need to reevaluate the design of present-day search systems.

We are suggesting the establishment of a state-of-the-art muon-proton and muon-nucleus collider that operates at the TeV level, capable of delivering highly accurate measurements in deep inelastic scattering in hadron physics. This type of collider would also enable the study of nucleus-muon interactions, making testableQCD and parton distribution functions accessible. From a particle physics perspective, it would enable the exploration of new physics beyond the Standard Model at the TeV scale. Additionally, we outline the main technical challenges involved in building such a facility, the necessary components, and outline the main stages of construction, before presenting a rough budget for this project.

A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR), yielding a semi-Lagrangian interpolation reconstruction method that accounts for respiratory motion. Nine human four-dimensional T2-weighted MR images, acquired without sequence optimization and comprising data corresponding to three distinct breathing phases, underwent multi-channel parallel imaging (auto-calibrating parallel acquisition with an acceleration factor of 2) and real-time reconstruction via a graphical processing unit. The influence of varying sampling points (from 150 to 290) on image quality in the four-dimensional images was evaluated after reconstruction with rCASPR. The outcome demonstrated acceptable mitigation of artifacts related to data under-sampling and motion interpolation, thereby confirming the feasibility of producing motion-compensated four-dimensional MRI data in reasonable time, within approximately 12 minutes (in-scan time), or after data post-processing.

This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing safety-critical controllers for complex nonlinear control systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a secure subset of possible system states and designs a control mechanism to maintain those states. The devised controller can be optimized through an efficiently solvable quadratic program, enabling real-time application. Building upon earlier concepts of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, ICCBFs demonstrate the ability to tackle a broader class of systems characterized by variable relative degrees. Finally, the paper showcases its efficacy through simulation examples in adaptive cruise control and spacecraft rendezvous.

In this work, domains are represented by equipping suitable families with an order based on set inclusion from specific mathematical structures. The focus here is on domain representations via approximation spaces enhanced with CF-approximable relations. Initially, we define the concept of CF-approximation spaces and establish the equivalence between CF-approximation spaces and a specific type of lattice structures - CF-distributions. Subsequently, we demonstrate that the collection of CF-approximation spaces forms a complete complex algebra, building on the foundation of CF-approximable relations. These CF-approximable relations provide the necessary framework for introducing operations such as binary and unary operators to CF-approximation spaces, which in turn enable the representation of cf-cyclic graphs and the construction of free structures above single generators.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples.

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the dissolution of shipping monopolies affected market behavior.

We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space.

Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Kedge, which involves explicitly reducing unnecessary graph edges by selectively removing neighboring nodes. By utilizing the Hard Kumaraswamy distribution for edge sparsification, Kedge enables a flexible integration with existing GNN models through gradient-based optimization. Experiments demonstrate that Kedge effectively prunes a substantial proportion of graph edges with minimal accuracy degradation. Notably, applying Kedge to the PubMed dataset resulted in the removal of over 99% of edges while achieving only a 1% decrease in accuracy. Furthermore, Kedge outperforms current state-of-the-art methods for GNNs with explicit dependencies, achieving comparable or superior accuracy while operating at significantly reduced computational cost.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches.

Building on previous findings, we observed in Part I that compact, singular areas within a manifold of positive scalar curvature can be conformally deformed to reveal related minimal geometries sharing key characteristics. This deformation preserves features like Ahlfors regularity, Poincare inequality validity, and tangent cones with positive scalar curvature. In Part II, we employ surgery-style arguments to successfully remove the singular sets present in these geometries.

A liquid consisting of superconducting vortices experiences an unusual response when subjected to a temperature and magnetic field that induces a thermal gradient. This reaction is characterized by a sudden increase in the transverse electric field that peaks at a specific point and then drops. This peak amplitude remains consistent across various types of superconductors despite their differences, which poses an interesting phenomenon to investigate further. This peak is essentially a representation of the minimum viscosity-to-entropy ratio in the vortex liquid, which in terms of units $\frac{\hbar}{k_B}$, is much greater than what is observed in common liquids. Moreover, there's a distinction to be made between the entropy held within the vortex core and the entropy bound to a moving magnetic flux line. A crucial aspect to consider here is that the entropy within the vortex core undergoes a continuous exchange with the surrounding normal quasi-particles due to a normal steady flow, which causes a decrease in the entropy bound within the core as the vortex moves at a slower speed. A vortex will eventually release all the entropy bound within its core within a specific distance, which is on the order of the coherence length of the superconducting material. This will occur provided that the ratio between the energy gap and the Fermi energy is sufficiently large.

Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions indicating optimal performance. The proposed PPC is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior outcomes compared to traditional MPC methods.

The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing inflation rates prompting people to invest in equities, commodities, and other assets, as opposed to saving. Deep Learning's ability to accurately predict time series data has been consistently demonstrated. In the realm of technical analysis, using indicators is the most widely adopted approach among traders and investors. Another essential aspect is sentiment analysis, reflecting the emotional state of investors' willingness to invest, where various techniques such as Machine Learning and Neural Networks have been employed. From simple linear regression to advanced neural networks, researchers and investors have experimented with multiple methods to forecast the stock market. It is evident from recent market fluctuations how news headlines and cryptocurrency prices are affected. This research paper presents an ensemble of state-of-the-art techniques to forecast stock prices. It begins with applying a BERT-based sentiment analysis model to analyze the emotional state of Apple Inc investors listed on NASDAQ. A subsequent GAN-based model predicts the company's stock price based on technical indicators, global stock indexes, commodity prices, and historical prices along with the sentiment scores. This model's performance is compared to benchmark models including LSTM, GRU, vanilla GAN, and ARIMA.

One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the outcomes of these events is challenging due to the intricate processes involved, such as mass and angular momentum transfer, object growth, and the release of radiation, including UV, X-rays, and massive particles. To assess the potential for CE events to merge, it is necessary to consider not only gravitational waves but also the potential for supernovae and gamma-ray bursts. This process involves calculating the CE merger probability, defined as the sum of the probabilities of producing at least one gravitational wave event, one supernovae, and one gamma-ray burst, or a combination of these outcomes. This probability can range from approaching 1 in some cases to approaching 0 in others, and it is influenced by factors such as the properties of the binary star system, such as the masses of the stars, the core mass of the primary star, and the angular momentum of the binary. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state.

We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of
$1/c^2$, considering a generic spacetime foliation defined by $c$, the speed
of light. We achieve this through the application of a suitable 'pre-non-
relativistic' geometrical parametrization, thereby facilitating an
analytical $1/c^2$ expansion of general relativity. Ultimately, this method
permits an in-depth examination of the Einstein-Hilbert action expansion up to
its next-to-next-to-leading order.

A new computational framework is introduced to speed up the calculation of localized shocks in a five-dimensional space that mimics anti-gravity, by simplifying the complex Einstein equations. It's discovered that using a first-order approximation yields highly accurate results, which can be broken down into two manageable sets of equations. Further, it's observed that one set has minimal impact on boundary measurements, allowing the calculation to be streamlined. This improvement results in significantly faster numerical solutions, with minimal errors, at roughly one-tenth the original time for specific conditions.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe.

Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles.

Over the years, the availability of data has expanded significantly thanks to advancements in computer technology and internet access, with a vast array of Linked Data now available for public use.  However, the sheer volume of data processing required to publish high-quality data has resulted in a significant number of poorly produced datasets that are riddled with inaccuracies, inconsistencies, and other errors.  Unfortunately, linked data quality assessment, verification, and correction tools are limited in scope compared to other data formats, making them ineffective in coordinating quality improvements across a wide range of datasets.  This paper proposes a new quality mark for Linked Data that incorporates the elements used in search engine result rankings, with a focus on developing an algorithm that can calculate these marks and enhance the efficiency of quality-assured datasets.  This algorithm, which can be integrated into existing quality improvement tools, is demonstrated using a dataset from music industry and shows significant increase in reach of low-quality datasets.

When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods without assumptions about a specific model typically lose efficiency, this paper introduces a robust procedure for estimating parameters in discrete data sets based on a well-known distance measure. Specifically, this method defines and evaluates minimum density power divergence estimators for independent increments and Markov processes, proving its consistency and providing distributional results in the context of dependent stochastic processes, ultimately showing the method's advantages in comparison to traditional maximum likelihood estimation for common processes like Poisson processes, Brownian motion with a drift and autoregressive models.

This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one kiloparsec of three high-brightness Seyfert galaxies. The findings from Gemini's GMOS-IFU data, acquired at a spatial resolution of 110-280 parsecs, reveal temperature variations of up to 10 times the differential average, with ranges from 6200K to 35000K. Our results also show temperature differences of up to 10000K between electrons and ions, indicating that the IFU scale captures a diverse range of plasma conditions. The temperature variations cannot be attributed to changes in ionizing photon energy alone, as demonstrated by previous research on another target. Our analyses highlight the complexity of nuclear plasma conditions and the need to reevaluate assumptions about broad spectral line formation. While mass outflows of 10 solar masses per year are observed in one target, magnetic fields capable of broadening spectral lines are implied in another, where outflows are not present.

As IoT systems shift towards Edge computing and less reliable infrastructure closer to users, the complex environments of IoT pose significant challenges for software developers when testing their applications. Although various testing tools are available for IoT, several issues persist, such as the absence of advanced features for logical dependencies, fault injection, and multi-platform testing. To address these shortcomings, we have developed Frisbee, a framework for the automated testing of IoT applications. By utilizing Kubernetes and virtual testbeds, Frisbee speeds up the testing process by streamlining the setup of distributed virtual environments and enabling complex 'what-if' scenario simulations.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$.

The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately mimic the distributions seen in real traffic environments. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real-world scenarios.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation.

A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs.
